endorsements.quote: Structured training is necessary to ensure they grasp how the technology functions, what its limitations are, and how to use it responsibly.

Structured training should include explicit instruction on how large language models process language, the common types of bias they may introduce, and how to identify and correct factual or contextual inaccuracies.
Ultimately, by actively editing and evaluating AI-generated notes, trainees not only have the opportunity to improve the quality of documentation but also deepen their understanding of patient care.

As emphasized by Gin et al (2025) in the New England Journal of Medicine, educators must help trainees “supervise” AI tools rather than defer to them—approaching AI outputs as drafts to be interrogated rather than conclusions to be accepted.
Before introducing AI scribes, learners must demonstrate their ability to independently write clear, accurate, and clinically meaningful notes.
In short, a mini-curriculum or course should be offered by training programs.

unlisted_practices: Require trainees to demonstrate independent note-writing competence, assessed individually by preceptors, before allowing AI scribe use.
Consider phased adoption with delayed access to the assessment portion of the note for trainees needing more experience.
Use AI-generated notes in coaching and feedback sessions for trainees to compare with their own notes and reflect on differences in reasoning and emphasis.
Encourage trainees to examine whether AI-generated notes capture the patient's voice and omitted social, emotional, and personal context.
Teach trainees to customize AI scribe templates and prompts intentionally to offload clerical tasks.

Do not use AI scribe transcripts as a replacement for faculty feedback; faculty may review transcripts for feedback only with trainee permission and with attention to ethical, legal, and psychological safety guidelines.

screen.reason: This is an editorial proposing seven best practices/guardrails for integrating AI scribes into medical residency training to preserve clinical reasoning.
